name: Nine oils (snake oil)

lead: Nine oils was a nineteenth-century liniment, first used on horses and later by people, rubbed into the skin to ease aches and bruises. Heavy laborers used it for back strains. In a training context it belongs to the family of rub-on remedies people turn to for sore muscles and joints, the idea being less discomfort and more consistent training.

The name did not always mean the same recipe. Snake oil, a related traditional liniment that came to mean a dubious cure, has been analysed in the Chinese water snake form for its omega-3 content, but no study has shown that these liniments work when rubbed on skin.

paras: Historically it was massaged into the sore area. The sources give no modern routines.

Historic recipes included turpentine, camphor, tar and even sulfuric acid, so irritation and burns were possible. Clark Stanley's snake oil liniment was found in 1916 to be mainly mineral oil and led to a fine.

chain: Liniment rubbed into sore muscles or joints
angle.text: People used nine oils to ease aches and back strains. For anyone building a physique, relief from soreness is the route to more consistent training.

lead: Nine oils was a nineteenth-century liniment, a preparation rubbed into the skin to relieve aches from bruises and strains. It seems to have been developed in veterinary medicine for horses and later adopted for people [1]. Laborers in heavy-lifting jobs trusted it for back strains; James Greenwood's 1883 Toilers in London described a street doctor selling sperm oil as the Nine [1].

A listed recipe in a nineteenth-century druggists' book named train oil, oil of turpentine, oil of bricks, oil of amber, spirit of camphor, Barbados tar and oil of vitriol, though many preparations sold under the name did not contain these and the name may never have referred to one formula [1].

Its link to looksmaxxing is the recovery theme: people use rub-on remedies for muscle and joint soreness hoping to train more comfortably and consistently. Snake oil, the better-known related liniment, was sold the same way and gave its name to a category of dubious remedies [2].
infobox: Veterinary use for horses, then human use [1]

paras: Nine oils appeared in the nineteenth century as a horse liniment before being used on people [1]. Greenwood's 1883 depiction shows laborers believing in it for back strains [1].

Snake oil liniments came from a different tradition. An unconfirmed story holds that Chinese laborers on the transcontinental railroad used Chinese water snake oil for aches, and a 1989 letter reported about 19.6% EPA in a sample of it, while rattlesnake fat had negligible omega-3 [2]. Clark Stanley, the Rattlesnake King, sold Snake Oil Liniment, and in 1916 the US Bureau of Chemistry found it mostly light mineral oil with about 1% fatty oil, capsaicin and possible traces of turpentine and camphor; he pleaded nolo contendere and was fined $20 [2]. The same article says no studies have shown snake oil is absorbed or effective as a liniment, and that massage or placebo effects may explain reported relief [2].
